title: Is Mumble Big or Small?
blurb: At breakfast, Mumble the little bear wants his mum's great big bowl, but the bowl is far too heavy. Then he has an idea: sort out the big things and the small things! In the end he says, “Just right for me!”

pages.text: Good morning! Mumble the little bear ran to the kitchen. Pitter pitter pat! Mama Bear was making breakfast. There was yoghurt and honey on the table. Mmm!

anne.say: Good morning, little one! Breakfast is ready.

pages.ask: What do you like to eat for breakfast in the morning?

pages.text: Mumble saw the great big bowl. “I'm big too! This one's mine!” He tried to lift it. Hnnngh! Too heavy! Mumble felt sad. His nose crinkled.

anne.say: Wait, little one, take a breath.

pages.ask: Why did Mumble feel sad? Have you ever tried to lift something very heavy? What happened?

pages.text: Mama Bear smiled. “Come, let's stand side by side.” Mama is great big, Mumble is tiny. The bowls are the same: one big, one small.

anne.say: Come, let's stand side by side.

predict.q: What do you think Mumble will do?

pages.ask: Who is bigger than you at home? What is smaller than you? How can you tell?

pages.text: Mumble had an idea. “Let's sort the dishes! Big ones for you, small ones for me!” Big or small? Hmm, hmm, hmm! Hop, hop!

mirmir.say: Big ones for you, small ones for me!

mech.done: Big ones for Mama, small ones for Mumble!

pages.ask: Whose is the big cup? Whose is the small cup? Why?

pages.text: Now the spoons! Mama Bear picked up the tiny spoon. “This is too small for me!” They both giggled. Big or small? Hmm, hmm, hmm!

anne.say: This spoon is too small for me!

mirmir.say: Hee hee! The tiny spoon is mine!

mech.done: Clink, clank! Every spoon found its place.

pages.ask: What would happen if Mama Bear ate with the tiny spoon?

pages.text: Mumble lifted the small bowl. Hop! Light as a feather! “Just right for me!” he said. Mama Bear laughed. “You grow a little every day.” Then they ate together. Gulp, gulp!

mirmir.say: Light as a feather! Just right for me!

anne.say: You grow a little every day.

pages.ask: What couldn't you do when you were little? What can you do now?

kazanim: MAB.4 Making inferences about mathematical facts, events and objects — MAB.4.b Compares objects: compares bowls, cups and spoons by size; uses the words “big–small” and “heavy–light”; compares Mumble's height with his mother's.

skill: KB2.5 Classifying: sorts tableware into two groups by a single feature (size) (big ones for Mama, small ones for Mumble) and matches the big spoon with the big bowl and the small spoon with the small bowl.

TADB.2 Building new meaning from what they hear: makes inferences from the story (why did the bowl feel heavy?) and links what is in the story to daily life (which is my cup, which is my spoon at home?).
SDB1.1 Self-awareness: notices their own size and strength; says what suits them (“Just right for me!”) and describes what they can do as they grow.
D2 Family Unity: notices that everyone in a family has different needs and enjoys eating together at the same table.
once: Look at the cover: “Which one is bigger, Mumble or his mum? How can you tell?”
Bring a big spoon and a small spoon from home and ask: “Which one is big, which one is small?”
Explain the words “heavy” and “light” by letting the child feel a book and a feather or a napkin.
sirasi: On page 1, run your fingers along your knee going “Pitter pitter pat!”
On page 2, look at Mumble's face: “How is he feeling? Why?” Take a breath together.
On page 3, after choosing a prediction, don't give the answer; say “Either one works” so both ideas count.
On page 4, let the child touch an item first and then its owner; say the chant “Big or small? Hmm, hmm, hmm!” together.
On page 5, while matching the spoon with its bowl, say the chant “Big with big, small with small.”
On page 6, let the child say the line “Light as a feather! Just right for me!” themselves.
sonra: What happened first in the story, and what happened next? Let's put the three pictures in order: the heavy bowl, the sorting, breakfast together.
Why couldn't Mumble lift the big bowl? What was the small bowl like? Why did his mum laugh at the tiny spoon?
Which things at home are “just right” for you?
Is there something you couldn't do last year but can do now?

sinif.ad: Big Bear, Little Bear Breakfast Table
sinif.materyal: Plastic bowls, cups and spoons in big and small sizes; two toy bears (one big, one small) or pictures of them; two baskets
adim: Put the items in a jumble in the middle of the rug; sit the two bears on either side.
The children take turns to choose an item, say “This is big/small” and put it in front of the right bear.
Match the spoons with the bowls; if someone puts a tiny spoon in the big bowl, laugh together and fix it.
The children stand back to back in pairs and compare heights: “Who is taller?” Stress: “Being tall or short is not good or bad; everyone grows at their own pace.”
Finally, each child completes the sentence “I can … !”

evSoru: Which bowl did Mumble want at breakfast?
Who got the big things, and who got the small ones?
What did Mumble say in the end?

evEtk.d: Set the table together. Let your child choose a plate, a cup and a spoon for each family member; talk about it: “Who is this for? Is it big or small?” Then eat together at the same table and tell your child you noticed their choices.

guide.aileNotu: Today we read “Is Mumble Big or Small?” Mumble the little bear wanted his mum's great big bowl but couldn't carry it; then he had an idea and sorted the things into big and small, and lifted the small bowl easily. The story supports comparing and grouping skills, and helps children get to know their own size and strength. At home, while setting the table, you can ask “Which one is big, which one is small?” and share the joy of growing by saying “You grow a little every day.”
